title: Why the United States Keeps Losing Wars
gist: Stephen Walt argues the US losing streak — Vietnam, Iraq, Afghanistan, Kosovo, and now Iran — has nothing to do with money, firepower or valor and everything to do with a structural mismatch: wars of choice pairing modest US interests with maximalist objectives, against opponents fighting for survival who therefore out-resolve Washington. He predicts the Iran war ends with Iran in a significantly stronger strategic position, and blames a foreign-policy elite that refuses to admit error, citing Robert Kagan's refusal to call the 2003 Iraq War a mistake.

insights.claim: Across many decades the United States' only clear military victory was the 1991 Gulf War, with Korea a draw and Vietnam, Iraq 2003, Afghanistan and Kosovo all failures or non-triumphs.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: One win in roughly seventy years is the base rate to apply to any new US military intervention thesis — including assumptions about a decisive outcome against Iran or China.
insights.quote: the United States’ only clear victory across these many decades was the 1991 Gulf War.
insights.locator: Look at the list.

insights.claim: The 1999 Kosovo War is counted as a non-triumph because Serbia obtained better terms at the end of the fighting than it had been offered before it began.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: A reminder that 'campaign concluded' is not 'objective achieved' — evaluate interventions on terms obtained versus terms available pre-war.
insights.locator: Look at the list.

insights.claim: The Cold War victory is an exception that proves the rule because it never involved a direct clash of arms with the Soviet Union, meaning US success correlates with not fighting.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Deterrence and containment have a far better US track record than warfighting — an argument for pricing US strategic competition with China through economic and alliance channels rather than kinetic ones.
insights.locator: Yes, I know: The United States and its allies did “win” the Cold War

insights.claim: The core failure mode is waging wars of choice that combine modest US interests with extremely ambitious goals such as remaking a foreign society in America's image.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: A screening test for any proposed US intervention: is the objective proportionate to the interest? Mismatch predicts failure regardless of force ratios.
insights.quote: The country has been waging wars of choice that combine modest U.S. interests with extremely ambitious goals, such as trying remake a foreign society in the U.S. image.
insights.locator: Instead, the real reasons that the United States keeps losing

insights.claim: Opponents are more highly resolved because they are fighting for survival or autonomy while the United States fights for desirable but less-than-vital objectives, producing an asymmetry in willingness to sacrifice.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Relative resolve, not relative capability, is the variable that predicts outcomes — apply it to Ukraine, Taiwan and Iran scenario analysis.
insights.locator: Instead, the real reasons that the United States keeps losing

insights.claim: In asymmetric conflicts the weaker side wins by not losing and outlasting the stronger power until it concludes the quagmire is not worth further soldiers and money.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Duration, not battlefield exchange ratios, is the metric that matters — long-war scenarios should be the base case for any US intervention.
insights.quote: the weaker side wins not by outright victory on the battlefield but by not losing
insights.locator: Under these conditions, it is to be expected

insights.claim: China sacrificed at least 200,000 troops in Korea because it saw US unification of the peninsula as an existential threat, illustrating how existential framing generates near-unlimited casualty tolerance.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Directly relevant to Taiwan: if Beijing frames a conflict as existential, historical precedent says its casualty tolerance vastly exceeds Washington's.
insights.quote: But China saw U.S. efforts to unify the peninsula as an existential threat, and eventually sacrificed at least 200,000 troops (and probably far more) to prevent that outcome.
insights.locator: This simple formula tells us a lot about all these recent wars.

insights.claim: American public support is the binding constraint that ended Vietnam, and leaders sustained it only temporarily by invoking exaggerated fears of falling dominos and lost credibility.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: US domestic polling is the real timeline governor on any extended conflict — a tradeable political variable for defense budgets and withdrawal timing.
insights.locator: In Vietnam, the United States faced the fierce nationalism

insights.claim: Iraq and Afghanistan followed the same pattern: Saddam was already contained with dismantled weapons programs and no 9/11 role, and Afghan nation-building triggered fierce resistance in a society deservedly called the graveyard of empires.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Regime removal was cheap; occupation was ruinous — the cost asymmetry between toppling and holding is the recurring miscalculation to watch for in any new intervention.
insights.locator: Much of the same fate drove the unfortunate outcomes

insights.claim: The 1991 Gulf War succeeded because US objectives were fully commensurate with US interests: expelling Iraq from Kuwait, decimating its military and imposing UN inspections, without occupying the country.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: The positive template: bounded objectives plus a prompt exit. Any intervention lacking a defined terminal condition should be assumed to fail.
insights.quote: Because U.S. aims were aligned with U.S. interests and Bush ended the war promptly, it is rightly seen as a stunning success.
insights.locator: The 1991 Gulf War is the obvious exception

insights.claim: George H.W. Bush's refusal to go to Baghdad was the decisive choice, avoiding both an overreach of the UN mandate and the occupation of a divided and resentful society.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: The counterfactual makes the mechanism explicit — the same war became a debacle in 2003 precisely by taking the step Bush declined.
insights.quote: But U.S. President George H.W. Bush wisely chose not to “go to Baghdad” and topple the regime
insights.locator: The 1991 Gulf War is the obvious exception

insights.claim: A superpower structurally struggles to align interests and objectives: being powerful and secure means few conflicts involve truly vital interests, while power and technological superiority make intervention look easy.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: The failure is systemic and self-reinforcing, not administration-specific — expect the pattern to persist across presidencies and party changes.
insights.quote: there won’t be a lot of conflicts where truly vital interests are at stake
insights.locator: It is not easy for a superpower to get its interests

insights.claim: Walt predicts the current war with Iran will end with Iran in a significantly stronger strategic position, having achieved none of the Trump administration's stated objectives.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: If correct, the postwar Middle East features a stronger Iran and diminished US deterrence — bearish for Gulf security premia normalizing and for US alliance credibility pricing.
insights.quote: This includes the current war with Iran, which has yet to achieve any of the Trump administration’s stated objectives and is likely to end with Iran in a significantly stronger strategic position.
insights.locator: If you’re an American, then you might be getting damn tired

insights.claim: Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have squandered the US supply of advanced missiles in the Iran war, measurably diminishing American strike capacity.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Depleted precision-munitions inventories are both a defense-procurement tailwind and a real constraint on US options in a simultaneous Pacific contingency.
insights.quote: given how U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have squandered the country’s supply of advanced missiles in their foolish war on Iran
insights.locator: Why has the United States done so poorly?

insights.claim: The pattern repeats even under a president who campaigned against forever wars and called himself the peace candidate, showing anti-interventionist rhetoric does not predict anti-interventionist behavior.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Discount campaign positioning on foreign policy entirely when forecasting intervention risk; structural incentives dominate stated intent.
insights.locator: Why does this keep happening, even under a president

insights.claim: The persistence of the pattern is driven by the US foreign-policy elite's refusal to hold itself accountable or learn from past mistakes.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Without an accountability mechanism, the error rate does not decay — assume future US intervention decisions carry the same failure probability as past ones.
insights.locator: There are many reasons, but one of them

insights.claim: Robert Kagan, a leading public advocate for the 2003 Iraq War, refused to call it a mistake, saying he was not sure what the utility of admitting it would be since it would not bring anyone back to life.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: A documented case of zero error-correction at the top of the advocacy chain — the specific evidence behind the structural claim.
insights.quote: I’m not sure what the utility of admitting that it was a mistake is. It’s not going to bring anybody back to life.
insights.locator: A perfect illustration of this problem

insights.claim: Kagan's stated main regret about Iraq is that the war reduced public support for the interventionist foreign policy he favors, not the war's consequences themselves.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Reveals the establishment's objective function is preserving interventionist capacity, which means advocacy for the next war is structurally unaffected by the last one's outcome.
insights.quote: He added that his main regret is that the war reduced public support for the kind of interventionist foreign policy that he favors.
insights.locator: When asked whether that war was a mistake

insights.claim: Repeated wrong wars for wrong objectives undermine allied confidence in US judgment and make it harder to compete with genuine rivals like China — the strategic cost is opportunity cost, not just casualties and money.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: Each Middle East entanglement is a transfer of strategic bandwidth to Beijing — the key second-order implication for long-horizon US-China competition positioning.
insights.quote: The problem is that it is usually fighting the wrong wars for the wrong objectives
insights.locator: The problem, in short, is not that the United States is bad at fighting wars.

insights.claim: Walt extends the accountability failure to much of the MAGA world, concluding Americans will have to get used to disappointment as long as the reluctance to admit error persists.
insights.speaker: Stephen M. Walt
insights.so_what: The diagnosis is bipartisan, so a change in Washington's governing coalition is not a catalyst for better strategic outcomes.
insights.quote: As long as a reluctance to admit errors and take responsibility remains widespread within foreign-policy circles—including much of the MAGA world at this point—Americans will have to get used to disappointment.
